description: Small things I am building outside work.
title: Building

content: My daughter asks "what's this?" about everything. The spoon. The dog on the street. The leaf that fell on the car. She is two. The world is a question. I wanted her to ask it in Kannada. Kannada is my mother tongue. It is the language I think in when I am tired. It carries the words my mother used. It is one of the ways my daughter will know where she comes from. I tried singing to her. I made hugs into songs. I read her books. She smiled and moved on. Then I noticed something. When she could match a word to an image, it stuck. She would say the word back. She would point. She would light up. That was the signal. So I built her an app I called it What's This in Kannada? It is an iOS app with a library of words. It includes animals, fruits, family members, and relationships. It has flashcards and a little quiz. There is voice, so when she asks "what's this?", I can pull up the app and let it answer. For the design, I pulled from something I already knew worked. There is a picture book she is obsessed with, one with warm, leafy illustrations full of animals. She could stare at those pages for twenty minutes. So I borrowed that world. The mascot is a squirrel. The palette is soft greens and browns. I designed the app so she can play for five minutes and then stop. I did not want an addiction loop or autoplay. I wanted a small, warm learning moment and then back to the world. I had never built an iOS app solo before this one. AI made it possible. I used AI in a specific way. I had a question at 10 p.m. after my daughter was asleep, and instead of waiting for the right tutorial or the right forum thread, I asked. I iterated. I got stuck. I asked again. The gap between "I have an idea" and something she can actually use keeps closing in a way it would not have a few years ago. That is the part that still surprises me, and the part that made this project possible. I learn by building, and AI gave me a way to keep going without stopping to wait. Still building The app is not out yet. I am still building it. There are words to add, edges to fix, and things I want to get right before I hand it to her for real. She has already used early versions, and she already has opinions. That tells me I am on the right track. The squirrel has more to do. Songs are next. Then stories. The little world we are building is just getting started.
description: A small iOS app I am building for my daughter, and what it taught me about language, product, and AI.
title: Building What's This in Kannada?

title: Writing

content: Not a resume dump. Not a perfect brand system. Just a place that felt like me. Somewhere I could publish when my mind was clear, not only when I happened to be at a desk. The AI era made that feel possible in a way it did not before. I am a mom. I like being outdoors. A lot of my best thinking happens while I am walking, or after bedtime, or in the small gaps where my hands are busy and my head is free. So I started working with voice notes. I talk. Agents listen. We turn the mess into something I can shape later. That became the workflow. Dogfooding my own learning One way I have been dogfooding what I am learning is simple. I make a list of projects I want to tackle. Then I actually try to do them. I try to think like an architect. Sometimes I work backwards from the outcome. I ask what the value is. I think about the path from idea to use, just enough to know why it should exist. Then I exercise the muscle that needs a little love. The engineering part. I use skills to grill me. I identify the architecture. I build prototypes. I evaluate. I get different models to cross-check each other. None of that is glamorous. It is just how I keep learning without waiting for a perfect stretch of uninterrupted time. From notes to a site All of that led me here. I started by trying to design the site with agents. I experimented with Design.md style prompts and a few structured design passes. That helped me think, but it did not give me the feeling I wanted. So I went back to the pen and paper way, in quotes. I looked at colors, made variations, and kept asking what felt like me. That is how the calm theme came together. Soft color, enough movement to feel alive, and no giant resume energy. I also wanted a dark mode because I am a developer experience person. Yes, I know developers love dark mode. For the build, Astro made sense because it is built for content-driven sites and keeps the page fast. Blume made sense because it let me keep writing in Markdown while still getting a production-grade site with navigation, theme, search, Open Graph images, and AI-readable output. That mattered to me. I wanted the writing to be easy for people to read and easy for AI tools to read. Then Codex helped me turn all of that into something real. I could describe the copy, the layout, the tone, and the changes I wanted. Then I could review, reject, rewrite, and keep going. This site came out of voice notes, Codex, Markdown, Astro, Blume, and a lot of editing. Still an MVP This site is still small. I will be back with more articles and small improvements. Thank you for being here.

title: How this site came together

content: It started with a simple question. Where am I losing time, and what would I do with that time if I got it back? I spend a lot of time thinking about how AI is changing developer workflows — how to make complex APIs easier to use, how to reduce friction, and how to help someone get from zero to a working integration faster. That curiosity leaked into my personal life. I started looking at the places where I was spending time on planning, sorting, remembering, and deciding. The answers were easy. Dinner walks with my family. Stories at bedtime. Making up songs and singing them badly. Tinkering with new ideas. Being a parent, a partner, and a person who is still figuring things out. So I started building with the tools in front of me. I run a fleet of agents on a local GPU. Each one has a clear job. Each one is sandboxed. Each one also has a personality, because that makes it easier for me to know when to use it and what kind of help to expect. There is a family assistant. There is a curriculum assistant that helps me think about what to teach my daughter. There is a health assistant that helps me look at my health metrics in the morning. There is a stock market analyzer. My favorite is Sherlock. Sherlock is my deep research assistant. The workflow is simple. I send Sherlock screenshots of things I see and want to understand. Sherlock researches them, breaks them down, and builds a report. I read those reports at bedtime. It has become one of the better habits I have built in a while. All of them live in Slack. They run around the clock. Some of them can talk to each other when a task needs more than one agent. I interact with them the way I would interact with a small team, except the team is there to help me think, plan, and follow through. Getting here was not clean. I failed a bunch of times before anything actually ran. There were architecture problems I could not solve alone, so I used stronger models to help me think through them. Things broke in ways I did not expect. Agents could not find each other. Nothing coordinated. I stopped trying to make the system perfect before using it. I shipped something rough. I fixed it. I shipped again. Now I am using the same system to plan birthday parties, which is probably the least glamorous use of agent infrastructure. But we have a lot of them coming up. There are gifts to find, parties to coordinate, and not much margin for error in a summer that is already moving fast. The Pacific Northwest summers are short. I want to be present for them. That is why I built this. I wanted to buy back a few hours a week and spend them on the things I care about. So far, it is working.
description: What a small Slack fleet is teaching me about time, presence, and imperfect systems.
title: Buying back time with a fleet of AI agents
